metadata.title: Using machine learning approaches to predict Taiwanese eighth graders' computational thinking performance in ICILS 2023 study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2023 microdata for Taiwan, with a two-stage sampling design: 169 junior high schools selected via stratified random sampling, followed by cluster sampling at the class level within selected schools. The analytic sample is restricted to Taiwanese 8th graders (n=5211) who completed the ICILS 2023 student questionnaire and the computational thinking (CT) performance test. The manuscript does not report applying ICILS sampling weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation pipeline, and it does not name any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the models are standard supervised classifiers trained in scikit-learn/XGBoost/LightGBM without explicit survey-weight integration, the results should be interpreted as predictive associations for the sampled students rather than fully population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a binary classification derived from standardized CT scores using the mean of the first plausible value (PV1) threshold from the ICILS international database. While the paper describes how the CT score threshold was set using PV1, it does not report any explicit missing-data rule for the 18 selected predictors (e.g., complete-case deletion or imputation). This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect both the training set composition and the stability of feature-importance estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the ICILS 2023 Taiwan dataset cleaned and pre-processed by IEA, restricted to Taiwanese junior high students in grade 8 (all participants were 8th graders; average age 14.3). The CT performance outcome was constructed from the ICILS CT test standardized scores, and the binary target was defined as below-average vs above-average using a threshold based on the mean of the first plausible value (PV1) from the ICILS international database. Predictors were further restricted to 18 derived indices/variables after aggregating overlapping/highly correlated items per IEA guidelines, removing variables with excessive missingness or weak theoretical connection, and screening for multicollinearity using VIF (retaining variables with VIF < 5).

confounders_identified.variable_name: Learning safe ICT use at school

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2023 Taiwan Grade 8 Computational Thinking (CT) test
main_findings.target_variable: CT performance (binary: below vs above average using PV1 threshold)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost — AUC: 0.79 (below-average and above-average), Accuracy: 0.72, Precision: 0.71, Recall: 0.74, F1-score: 0.72 (10-fold CV on 80% train; tested on 20% holdout).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2023 Taiwan Grade 8 Computational Thinking (CT) test the study leveraged CT disposition (CTDS), ICT self-efficacy (specialist), learning with specialist classroom apps, ICT self-efficacy (general), and academic media multitasking to predict CT performance (below vs above average using a PV1-based threshold), finding that XGBoost achieved the highest overall AUC (0.79) and strong classification performance (Accuracy 0.72, F1 0.72). This indicates that strengthening students’ CT disposition and specialist ICT self-efficacy—along with embedding specialist application use in classroom instruction—may improve CT achievement, though the binary target and lack of reported missing-data/weight handling limit causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes ICILS 2023 Taiwan data for 5211 grade-8 students, using the ICILS CT performance test (two randomly assigned CT modules) and the ICILS student questionnaire plus a 15-item CT disposition scale (CTDS). The CT outcome is converted into a binary classification (below vs above average) using a PV1-based threshold from the ICILS international database. Supervised ML classifiers (logistic regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, LightGBM, XGBoost, and a stacking ensemble) are trained with an 80/20 train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation, evaluated with AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. XGBoost and related ensembles reach AUC ≈ 0.79 and Accuracy ≈ 0.72, with top predictors identified via SHAP as CTDS, specialist ICT self-efficacy, and specialist classroom application learning. The paper does not report a missing-data strategy and does not document survey-weight use, so results should be treated as predictive associations rather than population-representative or causal effects.
